[MUQATIL:14:17/r1] MUQATIL, d. 150 · author | holds | The damned swallow the drink with great difficulty; “scarcely see it” in 24:40 means they do not see it at all. | mentions 24:40
[MUQATIL:14:17/r2] MUQATIL, d. 150 · author | holds | Death approaches from every direction in Hell, but they do not die; after twenty-one thousand years a gate called al-Hayhat opens, and further torment continues without relief.
[FARRA:v2p72/r1] FARRA, d. 207 · ابن عباس | reports | Ibn Abbas says الموت comes as punishment from before, behind, right, and left.
[FARRA:v2p72/r2] FARRA, d. 207 · إبراهيم التيمي | reports | Ibrahim al-Taymi explains يأتيه الموت من كل مكان as coming from every hair.
[FARRA:v2p72/r3] FARRA, d. 207 · author | holds | ميت describes an existing state, while مائت or ميت may describe what will die; Arabic uses the same present-state versus future-quality distinction in سيد/سائد and كريم/كارم.
[IBNQUTAYBA-GHARIB:v1p231#3/r1] IBNQUTAYBA-GHARIB, d. 276 · author | holds | Death reaches every place in the person's body, yet he does not die.
[IBNQUTAYBA-MUSHKIL:v1p119/r7] IBNQUTAYBA-MUSHKIL, d. 276 · author | holds | وراء means behind or in front: whatever is hidden from sight lies beyond one’s view; in two cited verses it means ahead of them.
[TAB-FULL:v13p617/r1] TAB-FULL, d. 310 · author | holds | For each tyrant, Hell is before him; وراء can mean “in front,” as the cited poem uses it.
[TAB-FULL:v13p617/r2] TAB-FULL, d. 310 · بعض نحويي أهل البصرة | reports | A Basran grammarian explains “before him” as what lies ahead of the present state, since the present is already past behind it; 18:79 uses the same sense. | mentions 18:79
[TAB-FULL:v13p617/r3] TAB-FULL, d. 310 · بعض نحويي أهل الكوفة | reports | A Kufan grammarian says this use is most common for times, which pass behind a person once experienced. | mentions 18:79
[TAB-FULL:v13p617/r4] TAB-FULL, d. 310 · بعضهم | reports | Another grammarian treats وراء as an opposite, able to mean either what is ahead or what is behind.
[TAB-FULL:v13p620/r1] TAB-FULL, d. 310 · author | holds | The damned sip the drink and can hardly swallow it because of its repulsiveness, yet thirst makes them swallow it.
[TAB-FULL:v13p620/r2] TAB-FULL, d. 310 · author | holds | Arabic uses لا يكاد both for something that happens, as here, and for something that does not, as in the verse about failing to see one’s hand. | mentions 24:40
[TAB-FULL:v13p620/r3] TAB-FULL, d. 310 · النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم | reports | The Prophet says that this drink cuts the drinker’s intestines until they exit through the anus. | mentions 47:15, 18:29
[TAB-FULL:v13p620/r4] TAB-FULL, d. 310 · النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم | reports | The same report links this punishment to boiling water that cuts bowels and to molten liquid that scorches faces. | mentions 47:15, 18:29
[TAB-FULL:v13p621/r1] TAB-FULL, d. 310 · author | holds | Death presses from every direction and every bodily part, but the sinner neither dies and rests nor lives in a way that brings relief because the soul is trapped at the throat.
[TAB-FULL:v13p621/r2] TAB-FULL, d. 310 · مجاهد | reports | Mujahid says the soul hangs at the throat, neither leaving so the person dies nor returning to the body to restore ease.
[TAB-FULL:v13p621/r3] TAB-FULL, d. 310 · إبراهيم التيمي | reports | Ibrahim al-Taymi says death reaches the unbeliever from beneath every hair on his body.
[ZAJJAJ:v3p156/r6] ZAJJAJ, d. 311 · author | holds | Yasīgh means to go down easily; the drinker cannot swallow the fluid, and waraʾahu in the final phrase means after it. 
[NAHHAS:v2p365/r2] NAHHAS, d. 338 · author | holds | Angels force the damned to swallow the drink; it barely passes the throat, death comes from every bodily place, and another torment may follow.
[HAMASA:v1p490/r1] HAMASA, d. 421 · author | holds | The object of aqūlu is in the first hemistich of the following verse, beginning with بك الوجبة.
[HAMASA:v1p490/r10] HAMASA, d. 421 · author | holds | Awmada and wamada both mean to gleam; the variant reading minaya al-mawt in place of thanaya al-mawt is a corruption.
[HAMASA:v1p490/r11] HAMASA, d. 421 · author | holds | Ajl al-qatilin uses a part for the whole and repeats the name for emphasis; the first Ajl may be nominative with the second accusative as apposition or clarification.
[HAMASA:v1p490/r12] HAMASA, d. 421 · author | holds | Banu Ajl were owed blood revenge by the poet's tribe, Banu Mazin, but killed an uninvolved stranger from Yuhsab who had been staying with them.
[HAMASA:v1p490/r13] HAMASA, d. 421 · author | holds | The poet mocks Banu Ajl for claiming revenge when they killed a foreign guest who had neither sought nor helped win the blood debt.
[HAMASA:v1p490/r14] HAMASA, d. 421 · author | holds | The poet's use of zʿamtum may undermine their claim to have taken their right, their supposed revenge, or both; al-Marzūqi says the last reading is most apt.
[HAMASA:v1p490/r15] HAMASA, d. 421 · author | holds | The two objects of zaʿamtum are omitted, as in the Qur'anic question about alleged partners. | mentions 28:62
[HAMASA:v1p490/r2] HAMASA, d. 421 · author | holds | The poet uses the plural mafāriq for the areas around the crown, treating each part by the parting as its own parting.
[HAMASA:v1p490/r3] HAMASA, d. 421 · author | holds | Khar means fell, with the verbal noun khurur; suhuq describes a tall palm or donkey.
[HAMASA:v1p490/r4] HAMASA, d. 421 · author | holds | The fallen man is compared to a trunk, a familiar simile; al-Marzūqi cites the Qur'anic image of hollow palm trunks and notes that this makes his height vivid. | mentions 69:7
[HAMASA:v1p490/r5] HAMASA, d. 421 · author | holds | The speaker says he felled a mighty man with his sword, then taunts him that the great death blow settled on him, not on the person he had sought.
[HAMASA:v1p490/r6] HAMASA, d. 421 · author | holds | Al-wajba al-uzma means death; the cited Qur'anic phrase describes sacrificial camels falling on their sides. | mentions 22:36
[HAMASA:v1p490/r7] HAMASA, d. 421 · author | holds | Fa-abid is a contemptuous prayer against the fallen man; malhab can mean humbled or, alternatively, wounded and cut lengthwise.
[HAMASA:v1p490/r8] HAMASA, d. 421 · author | holds | A second line likens a drawn sword's flash to the gleaming teeth of death, and al-Marzūqi calls this more eloquent than the earlier image.
[HAMASA:v1p490/r9] HAMASA, d. 421 · author | holds | This poet makes death's smile the sword's flash as it leaves the sheath, delighted and confident it will strike the victim.
[HAMASA:v1p73/r1] HAMASA, d. 421 · author | holds | Al-fatik is one who surprises another with harm or killing; a hadith calls faith a restraint on treacherous attack, and al-Duraydi says the term is for someone who acts once resolved.
[HAMASA:v1p73/r10] HAMASA, d. 421 · author | holds | Al-Marzūqi compares another poem's image of death reaching from every lookout and says it describes the sword and its wielder's force.
[HAMASA:v1p73/r11] HAMASA, d. 421 · author | holds | The poet's reference to a bone of a peer signals that he only confronts someone comparable in courage; attributing the grin to molars is figurative, and al-dawāhik are the teeth that show when laughing.
[HAMASA:v1p73/r2] HAMASA, d. 421 · author | prefers | The alternate wording describing enemy footmen appearing and prompting him toward drawing his sword is the more reliable of the two recensions.
[HAMASA:v1p73/r3] HAMASA, d. 421 · author | holds | Al-adi means the foot soldiers who run ahead of the cavalry; it is a collective form like al-kalib and al-da'in.
[HAMASA:v1p73/r4] HAMASA, d. 421 · author | holds | On the first recension, the eye is the heart's lookout, ready to expose and correct what the heart dislikes, especially by watching for the sword to be drawn.
[HAMASA:v1p73/r5] HAMASA, d. 421 · author | holds | Al-Marzūqi answers that the lines describe two states: the first is sleep, when the heart stays alert, and the second is wakefulness, when the eye guards the heart.
[HAMASA:v1p73/r6] HAMASA, d. 421 · author | holds | Al-akhlaq means smooth, and al-batik means cutting.
[HAMASA:v1p73/r7] HAMASA, d. 421 · author | reports | In ila salla, ila can mean with, or it can mark the endpoint: the eye keeps watch until he draws the sword, after which action belongs to the heart.
[HAMASA:v1p73/r8] HAMASA, d. 421 · author | holds | The phrase min haddi akhlaq is an expansive expression: the sword is drawn from its sheath and thereby becomes unsheathed, like idioms that place clothing into a body part.
[HAMASA:v1p73/r9] HAMASA, d. 421 · author | holds | The sword's motion makes death seem to grin at a formidable opponent, personifying death as certain of striking its target; the teeth image depicts its glee.
[THALABI:v5p310/r10] THALABI, d. 427 · author | holds | He is not dead, so he cannot release his soul and rest.
[THALABI:v5p310/r11] THALABI, d. 427 · ابن جريج | reports | Ibn Jurayj says the soul remains at the throat, unable to leave and cause death or return to the body and restore life. | mentions 20:74
[THALABI:v5p310/r12] THALABI, d. 427 · author | holds | The final phrase means another severe punishment awaits after this torment.

[THALABI:v5p310/r3] THALABI, d. 427 · ابن عباس | reports | Ibn Abbas says they do not like the drink; another view says the same.
[THALABI:v5p310/r4] THALABI, d. 427 · أبو أمامة | reports | Abu Umama transmits a Prophetic report: when the drink nears the condemned, it burns his face and scalp, then severs his intestines as he swallows it.
[THALABI:v5p310/r5] THALABI, d. 427 · author | holds | The text links the hot drink severing intestines and the burning of faces to other Qur'anic descriptions. | mentions 47:15, 22:20
